claim: MTD changes a network's addresses, layout and software
quote: Many MTD techniques, including Internet Protocol (IP) mutation, network topology changes, platform migration, and software stack shuffling, change the attack surface

claim: MTD changes a network's credentials, so that stolen credentials go out of date
quote: The example system or network attributes that can be changed include instruction sets [95], [132], address space layouts [144], IP addresses [3], [12], [87], [97], [147], port numbers [107], proxies [91], virtual machines [22], [177], operating systems [157], or software programs [84].
locator: Sec. III-B 'What to move', p. 713 printed (PDF p. 5)
issue: Cho's list of moving attributes has no credentials; its only credential mention is redundancy requiring 'additional credentials' (p. 716 printed), not rotating them. Nothing in Cho says stolen credentials go out of date.
fix_text: cite a source for credential rotation as MTD, or cut 'and credentials' and 'stolen credentials and' from the cho2020-cited sentence

claim: MTD changes these on a schedule, so reconnaissance goes out of date even if the attacker is never detected
quote: The proactive adaptation triggers MTD techniques by changing configurations or properties on a schedule, with either fixed or random intervals between adaptations. Proactive adaptations ensure that any information gained by the
locator: Sec. III-B 'When to move', pp. 713-714 printed (PDF pp. 5-6), continuing 'attacker quickly expires [110] ... Proactive MTD moves regardless of the presence of an attacker'
issue: Cho says this of proactive MTD only; it also defines reactive MTD, which moves on detection. The sentence states it of MTD in general.
fix_text: 'changes ... on a schedule' -> 'can change ... on a schedule', or name proactive MTD; the simplification may be acceptable for ch1

claim: Most MTD tests run in simulation
quote: Most studies evaluating the performance of MTD approaches have been validated based on simulation experiments.
issue: Cho is a 2020 survey; the present tense leans on its currency, which jalowski2026 in the same bracket covers.

claim: Most tests run against attacker models far simpler than an APT
quote: highly intelligent, learning attackers are not really considered. Generally, it is assumed that attackers have certain attack patterns, rather than that they learn and can launch adaptive attacks.
locator: Sec. V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15); also Sec. X 'beyond the reconnaissance stage', p. 738 printed (PDF p. 30)
issue: Cho names specific gaps (non-learning attackers, single attacks, reconnaissance stage) but never compares attacker models with an APT, and reports that APT attacks are among the three attacks existing MTD 'mainly addressed' and that existing MTD attackers 'are persistent' (p. 720). 'far simpler than an APT' is the dissertation's synthesis.
fix_text: 'far simpler than an APT' -> 'simpler than an APT', or let jalowski2026 alone carry the APT comparison

claim: No standard set of MTD metrics exists
quote: However, no standard metrics have been proposed to measure their effectiveness and efficiency.
locator: Sec. VII opening, p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19)
issue: Wording matches, but the source is a 2020 survey; the present-tense claim in 2026 rests on currency the source cannot give. The 2026 survey cited in the next sentence would carry the present tense if it says so.
fix_text: add jalowski2026 to 'No standard set of metrics exists', if it states the absence

claim: Cho lists attack success probability (ASP) as an attacker-side effectiveness metric
quote: Attack success probability (ASP) [3], [11], [22], [25], [26], [28], [32], [45], [49], [136], [147], [173]: This metric refers to the probability that attacks are successfully performed.

claim: Cho lists MTTC as an attacker-side effectiveness metric
quote: Mean time to compromise a system (MTTC) [4], [26], [27], [32], [186]: This indicates how long an attacker takes to compromise an entire system.

claim: Cho lists attack utility as an attacker-side effectiveness metric
quote: Attack utility [5], [6], [22], [119], [134], [181], [182]: When the interactions between attackers and defenders and their best strategies are considered based on game theoretic approaches, the payoff (or utility) of an attacker is used to measure the gain or loss by deploying a proposed MTD.

claim: Cho lists defence success probability as a defender-side effectiveness metric
quote: Defense success probability (DSP) [3], [35], [38], [173]: We call metrics measuring the success of an MTD technique DSP in this work.

claim: Analytical models are the cheapest evaluation method to evaluate
quote: The evaluation of probabilistic models provides insights and lessons based on the observations of general system behaviors with minimum evaluation cost.
issue: Cho says 'minimum evaluation cost' of probabilistic models only; for graphical security models (the other analytical kind) it gives 'ease of evaluation' but a scalability issue. No superlative across the four methods.
fix_text: defensible reading of Sec. VIII; at most 'cheap to evaluate but abstract'

claim: Analytical models are the most abstract evaluation method
quote: due to the probabilistic parameterization of all the key system design features, a certain level of simplicity and abstraction is unavoidable
issue: Cho says abstraction is unavoidable in probabilistic models, and elsewhere that analytical or simulation models both 'inherently' introduce abstraction (Sec. IX-A); it never ranks analytical as 'the most' abstract.

claim: Emulations and real testbeds are the most realistic evaluation methods
quote: Emulation models can provide a higher validity than simulation models in the experimental results validated through them.
locator: Sec. VIII-C, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23); real testbeds 'more realistic system environments', Sec. VIII-D, p. 732 printed (PDF p. 24)
issue: Cho gives comparatives, not a superlative, and does not rank emulation level with real testbeds.

claim: Emulations and real testbeds are hard to scale to large networks
quote: most emulation-based test environments (e.g., Mininet) running on a single machine share the same hardware resources for all emulation elements, making it difficult to evaluate experiments for large-scale networks.
locator: Sec. VIII-C, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23); real testbeds 'it is difficult to evaluate the MTD techniques in large-scale networks', Sec. VIII-D, p. 732 printed (PDF p. 24)

claim: Cho's finding is that MTD attacker models in general lack the properties of an APT attacker
quote: In the existing MTD works, we found that attackers are persistent, not performing a one-time attack (e.g., APT attacks [22], [45], [49], [78]).
locator: Sec. V-A, p. 720 printed (PDF p. 12); the limitations are Sec. V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Cho's limitations are specific (learning attackers, multiple strategies, attacks beyond reconnaissance are under-considered), while it also reports that existing MTD attackers are persistent and that APT is one of the three attack types MTD mainly addresses. 'lack the properties of an APT attacker' in general overstates Cho and partly conflicts with it.
fix_text: 'lack the properties of an APT attacker' -> 'lack several properties of an APT attacker'
